title: Boredom is a skill.
dek: Twelve gaps of three minutes a day add up to almost two waking weeks a year. Most of them now have a screen in them, and the mind that used to wander there has nowhere to go.
whyThisIdea: Este următoarea idee nefolosită din backlog (am sărit peste „Why people quit in week three”, prea aproape de „Motivation is a mood” - același studiu Lally și aceeași idee de motivație care scade). Se leagă de articolul despre telefon și de cel de ieri despre notițe: ce pierzi în micile pauze pe care le umple ecranul.

entry.title: Boredom is a skill.
entry.dek: Twelve gaps of three minutes a day add up to almost two waking weeks a year. Most of them now have a screen in them, and the mind that used to wander there has nowhere to go.
body: “A generation that cannot endure boredom will be a generation of little men.” — Bertrand Russell

Have you ever asked yourself when was the last time you were really bored? Not “this lesson is long” bored, but bored with nothing in your hands - no phone, no music, nothing to read, just you and a few minutes that nobody filled. I tried to remember mine this morning, waiting for the kettle, and I could not. The phone was already in my hand before the water was hot. So the question is: if boredom feels so bad, why do I have the feeling that I am losing something by never feeling it? Let’s start from the beginning.

The thing I want to look at is the small gap. The queue at the shop, the bus that is four minutes late, the 40 seconds before the teacher walks in, the ad before the video. A few years ago these were empty moments. Now every single one of them has a screen in it, and I do not even decide to take the phone out, my hand does it for me. In the article about “just checking” I wrote about what the phone costs when you are trying to work. This is the other side of it: what it takes from the moments when you were not doing anything at all.

Firstly, let’s split “boredom is a skill” in two, the way I like to do with a title. “Boredom” is a feeling, and not a nice one, nobody is arguing that. But “skill” is the interesting word, because a skill is something you get better at when you practise it and worse at when you stop. And I think that is exactly what happened to me: I did not stop getting bored, I stopped being able to stand it. In 2014, Timothy Wilson and his colleagues at the University of Virginia published a study in Science with a very simple setup. They left people alone in a room for 6 to 15 minutes with nothing to do but think, and most of them did not enjoy it. Then they made it stranger. Before being left alone, people tried a small electric shock and said they would even pay money not to get it again. Then they sat alone for 15 minutes with a button that gave them that same shock. 12 of the 18 men (67%) and 6 of the 24 women (25%) pressed it at least once (yes, you read that right, the shock they had just said they would pay to avoid). For a lot of people, pain was better than nothing.

Secondly, let’s do the arithmetic on the gaps, because one of them looks like nothing. These numbers are my own guesses for a normal day of mine, not a study. Say there are 12 small gaps in a day - queues, waiting, walking between classes - and each one is about 3 minutes.
12 × 3 minutes = 36 minutes a day
36 minutes × 365 days = 13.140 minutes, or 219 hours a year
219 hours ÷ 16 waking hours a day = almost 14 waking days
So in my own example, about two waking weeks a year come in pieces of three minutes. Nobody would give away two whole weeks of their life to a screen on purpose. But nobody gives them away on purpose, we give them away 3 minutes at a time, and no single gap ever feels big enough to protect.

And what was in those gaps before? I think it was the mind wandering, the thing that happens when there is nothing to hold on to. In 2014, two psychologists from the University of Central Lancashire, Sandi Mann and Rebekah Cadman, asked people to do something very boring on purpose: copy numbers out of a phone book for 15 minutes. After that, they had to come up with as many uses as they could for two plastic cups. The bored group came up with more ideas than the group that went straight to the cups. In a second study, just reading the numbers, which is even more boring than copying them, worked even better. <u>Boredom is not an empty room, it is the room where the mind starts looking around.</u> Some of the ideas for this blog came exactly from moments like that, on a walk without headphones, and none of them came while I was scrolling.

Thirdly, and this is the counter-case I have to be fair to. Not every boredom is useful. Being bored for a whole afternoon because you have nothing to do and nobody to see is not a creative superpower, it is just a bad afternoon, and for some people it is a lot worse than that. So I do not want to say that boredom is good. What I want to say is smaller: being able to sit through a few boring minutes without running away from them is a skill, and like any skill, if you never use it, you lose it. It is the same muscle you need for a hard chapter, a slow workout or a long problem at school, all the moments where the first few minutes are boring and the good part comes only if you stay.

So here is what I am going to do, because an article like this is worthless if it ends only in agreement. Starting today, a Wednesday, I will pick one gap every day where the phone stays in my pocket - one queue, one walk, one bus. Not the whole day, just one gap. And if something comes into my head while I am standing there doing nothing, I will write one sentence about it when I get home. At the end of the month I will read those sentences and see if the empty minutes gave me anything, or if they were just empty.

For today, that will be all. My personal opinion? I believe the idea is right, but I have to be honest about the evidence and about myself. The Wilson study was an empty room with nothing in it, which is not the same as a bus stop, and the groups were small. The cups study measured ideas for cups, not ideas for your life. And it is very easy to romanticise boredom while writing on a laptop - a screen in a queue is sometimes a message to your grandmother or ten minutes of a language, and that is not a loss at all. I also like my phone, I am not going to pretend otherwise. What I take from it is smaller: the problem is not the phone in the gap, it is that I no longer remember choosing it.
In the end, I hope you enjoyed this article and I will leave you with the line that started all of this. Peace!
